en: The Sūtra on Entering the Seal of Entering the Non-Determinate State, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Therein, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, and sixty billion, hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas. Their names were:

the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, and Nityaghosarāja Bodhisattva. With these as their leaders, there were sixty billion, hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained the samādhi of the supernatural power of tranquil debate, the śūraṅgama-vikrāmiṇa samādhi, and the samādhi of the ocean tide not exceeding its limit; they had attained the dhāraṇī of receiving empowerment, and the dhāraṇī of gathering the ultimate physical forms and colors of infinite Buddhas.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, expound the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Wisdom for entering the state of certainty and non-certainty."

By means of that seal, may I know for certain whether this bodhisattva is destined or not destined, and whether this one who is not destined will fall back from unexcelled perfect enlightenment and the path to supreme wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī, herein there are five kinds of bodhisattvas.”
What are these five? First, the practice of the sheep-vehicle;

second, the practice of the elephant-vehicle; third, the practice of the supernatural vehicle of the moon and sun; fourth, the practice of the supernatural vehicle of the śrāvakas; and fifth, the practice of the supernatural vehicle of the Tathāgatas.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the five kinds of bodhisattvas. Mañjuśrī!
The first two bodhisattvas are not necessarily destined for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and may regress from the path of supreme wisdom.
The latter three bodhisattvas are necessarily destined for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and do not regress from the path of supreme wisdom.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
Which two bodhisattvas are not yet fixed in their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and thus retreat from the path of supreme wisdom?”
“World-Honored One!
Which three types of bodhisattvas are certain to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will not regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom?
The Buddha said:

“Mañjuśrī! The bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of sheep and the bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of elephants—these two types of bodhisattvas are not certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.”

Mañjuśrī! The bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the moon and sun, the bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the śrāvakas, and the bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata—these three types of bodhisattvas are certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall not regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī! How should one know a bodhisattva who practices the sheep vehicle? Mañjuśrī!”

For example, suppose there were a person who, for some reason, for a great reason, for some purpose, for a great purpose, out of some regard, or out of great regard, wished to pass beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in five hundred Buddha-worlds in other directions in order to reach that place.
He reflects thus:
"By what vehicle may I pass beyond such worlds and reach that place?
Thereupon, that person reflects as follows:
"If I were now to mount a sheep-cart, I would be able to pass through such worlds and reach that place.
Mañjuśrī! Having reflected thus, that person mounts the sheep-cart and sets out upon that path.
After traveling for a long time until it had reached one hundred yojanas, a great wind-circle arose and blew it back eighty yojanas.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Could such a person, riding that sheep-cart, pass through and reach that world?
Whether it takes one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or a hundred billion kalpas, or even unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—could that person pass beyond a single world-system?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“World-Honored One!
It is impossible for him to pass beyond even a single world-system.”

If such a person were to ride that sheep-cart, even if they traveled for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, it would be impossible for them to pass beyond a single world-system.
The Buddha said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, should dwell in association with followers of the *śrāvaka-yāna*—approaching those of the *śrāvaka* vehicle, training under them, honoring and making offerings to those of the *śrāvaka-yāna*, and forming friendships with them; if they share their wealth and live together with them;
if they practice in the same locations as them, whether in forests, monasteries, or places for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*);

if they read the *śrāvaka-yāna*, recite the *śrāvaka-yāna*, contemplate the *śrāvaka-yāna*, and believe in the *śrāvaka-yāna*, and furthermore teach others to read, recite, contemplate, and believe in it.

Such a person dwells in the Śrāvaka-yāna, gathering the roots of goodness and practices of the Śrāvaka-yāna; because they are led by the Śrāvaka path, they attain dull wisdom and retreat from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.

In this way, if a bodhisattva who has cultivated the faculty of wisdom and the eye of wisdom of the bodhicitta later dwells in the knowledge of a śrāvaka and practices the cultivation of roots of goodness therein, they will once again become dull-witted, ruined, and fail to achieve success.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there is a person who suffers from an eye disease or has blurred vision; for the sake of opening their eyes, this person undergoes medical treatment diligently and without rest for one month, and after that month has passed, their eyes have opened slightly.”

There was an enemy who constantly watched for an opportunity; he took crushed *bibhītaka* seeds and placed them in the man's eyes, causing his vision to grow increasingly dark until his eyes closed and could no longer open to see clearly.
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva cultivates the bodhicitta,

the faculty of wisdom, and the eye of wisdom, yet at a later time dwells in the knowledge of a śrāvaka and practices the cultivation of roots of goodness therein, he will then become dull-witted, ruined, and fail to achieve success."
“Mañjuśrī! This should be known as the bodhisattva who practices the sheep-cart vehicle. Mañjuśrī!”
"How should one know a bodhisattva who travels by means of an elephant vehicle? Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person who, for some purpose—whether it be a cause, a great cause; an action, a great action; or a priority, a great priority—desired to pass beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in order to reach that place."
He reflects thus:
"By what vehicle may I cross over such worlds and reach that place?
Such a person then reflects in this way:
"If I were now riding upon an elephant-vehicle endowed with the eightfold qualities, I would be able to pass through such worlds as these to reach that place. Mañjuśrī!

Once that person has completed such reflection, he mounts an eightfold-proportioned elephant carriage and sets out upon that path; though he travels two thousand yojanas constantly for a hundred years, a great wind-circle arises and blows him back one thousand yojanas.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would such a person,
riding upon that elephant vehicle, be able to traverse a single world-system?

Whether it be for one kalpa, or one hundred kalpas, or one thousand kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—could that person pass beyond a single world-system?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"World-Honored One!
It is impossible for him to pass beyond even a single world-system."

If such a person were to ride that elephant vehicle for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, it would be impossible for them to pass beyond even a single world-system.
The Buddha said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dwells in the company of those of the *śrāvaka-yāna*, stays near them, associates with them, and forms friendships with them;
if they walk together in the same place— whether in a forest, a monastery, or a place for walking meditation—

and read the *śrāvaka-yāna*, recite the *śrāvaka-yāna*, contemplate the *śrāvaka-yāna*, and believe in the *śrāvaka-yāna*, and furthermore teach others to read, recite, contemplate, and believe in it.

Such a person dwells in the wisdom of the śrāvaka, gathering the roots of goodness and practices of the śrāvaka vehicle; because they are led by the śrāvaka path, they attain dull wisdom and regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.

In this way, when a bodhisattva cultivates the bodhicitta, plants roots of goodness, and practices while abiding in the Mahāyāna, yet later dwells in the wisdom of a śrāvaka and plants roots of goodness there, they will instead become dull-witted, fall into ruin, and fail to achieve their goal.
“Mañjuśrī! It is like a great log, a thousand yojanas in breadth, adrift upon the great ocean, ferrying sentient beings across the sea.
A yakṣa who travels through the air takes it out and places it on land, binding it to a massive iron block five hundred yojanas in size.”
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
Could such a great log ever be carried away by the waters of that great ocean?
"Furthermore, can you rescue sentient beings within the ocean?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I cannot."
The Buddha said: "So it is, Mañjuśrī!"

If that bodhisattva, while cultivating the practices for planting roots of goodness through the bodhicitta and practicing the path to the knowledge of all modes of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), is led astray and causes them to regress, they will be unable to advance upon the path to the great ocean of omniscience, nor will they be able to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the great ocean of birth and death.
Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva who practices this elephant-vehicle path should know this. Mañjuśrī!
"How should one know a bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural power of the moon and sun? Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person who, for some purpose—whether it be a cause, a great cause; an action, a great action; or a priority, a great priority—desired to pass beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in order to reach that place."
He reflects thus:
"By what vehicle can I pass beyond such worlds and reach that place?
This person then reflects accordingly.
"Mañjuśrī! If I were now to mount the supernatural vehicle of the moon and sun, I should be able to pass through such worlds and reach that place."
Once such a person has reflected in this way, they immediately set out upon that path by means of the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the moon and sun.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
"Could such a person, riding upon the vehicle of the supernatural power of the sun and moon, pass through and reach that world?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"After a long time, one will be able.
The Buddha said, "It is so."

Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not dwell in association with any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not draw near to any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not associate with any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not act as their spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); does not exchange wealth or goods with them; and does not cohabit with them;
whether in a forest, a monastery, or a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), he does not walk in the same place as they do.

Furthermore, they do not recite or chant the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle; they do not contemplate or believe in the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor do they instruct others to recite, believe, or study them. They do not even learn, read, or chant so much as a single verse.
If that person reads, they read the Mahāyāna; if they recite, they recite the Mahāyāna; and if they have anything to say, they speak of the Mahāyāna, even if it be but a single verse.
Mañjuśrī! This is the practice of the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the moon and sun; bodhisattvas should know this. Mañjuśrī!
It is, for example, as if there were a great Garuḍa king, powerful and in the prime of youth, who could go from the summit of Mount Sumeru to another place according to his will; even so, even so.

Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural power of the sun and moon possesses the great strength of precepts, learning, and profound resolve; being youthful, courageous, and capable, they can reach all Buddha-worlds according to their mental recollection of Buddhas, manifesting their bodies within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas.
“Mañjuśrī! How should one know a bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the śrāvakas? Mañjuśrī!”

Suppose there were a person who, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms, had a cause and a great cause, an action and a great action, a priority and a great priority; for the sake of that matter, he desired to pass through as many worlds as there are atoms to reach that place.
He reflects thus:
"By what supernormal power can I pass through such worlds and reach that place?
Thereupon, that person reflects as follows:
"I shall now, by means of the supernatural powers of a śrāvaka, pass through such worlds as these and reach that place.
Mañjuśrī! Having thus reflected, that person immediately mounts the supernatural powers of a śrāvaka and sets out upon that path.
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
Can such a person, by means of the supernatural powers of a śrāvaka, travel across to that world?
Mañjuśrī replied, “One can transcend it.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not dwell in association with any followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna; does not draw near to any followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna; does not cultivate intimacy with any followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna; does not act as their kinsman, does not exchange wealth or goods with them, does not practice together with them, does not converse with them, and does not cohabit with them;
Whether in a forest, in a monastery, or on a walking path, one does not practice in the same place [as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle];

one does not read or recite the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle; one does not contemplate or believe in the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle; one does not instruct others to read or recite even a single verse of it, nor does one engage in recitations inconsistent with the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor teach others to do so.

If that person reads, they read the Mahāyāna; if that person recites, they recite the Mahāyāna; they also teach others to read and recite the Mahāyāna, and whatever they speak, they speak of the Mahāyāna.

Toward those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have faith and resolve in the Mahāyāna—those who read the Mahāyāna, recite the Mahāyāna, and uphold the Mahāyāna—he respects them with right faith, follows and trains in accordance with them, associates with them without ever abandoning them, relies upon and stays close to them, makes offerings to them in accordance with the Dharma, regards them as spiritual friends, and dwells together with them;
whether in the forest, in a monastery, or on a walking path, he practices alongside them.

Toward those who belong to the Mahāyāna, who embrace the Mahāyāna, who have received the Mahāyāna, and who uphold the Mahāyāna, one should offer the highest respect and the most excellent worship—namely, lamps, various flowers, incense, powdered incense, unguents, and exquisite garlands for anointing the body—and thus perform such offerings.

Such a person, having read and recited the Mahāyāna, speaks to others with the foremost joyful mind; they do not hold those bodhisattvas who have not yet studied in contempt, but address them with a favorable countenance, greeting them first with kind words. They do not utter evil speech or coarse and harsh language, but always speak words of affection and speak words that are beautiful and sublime.

Such a person will not abandon the Mahāyāna even for the sake of losing their life or facing death; they will always gather in all those who practice the Mahāyāna, study the Mahāyāna, read the Mahāyāna, recite the Mahāyāna, and uphold the Mahāyāna, gathering them according to their capacity, according to the Dharma, and according to what their minds are able to bear.
Such a person is not hated by anyone and has no one with whom to contend; they constantly seek all sūtras never heard before, their mind always honoring and respecting those from whom they hear them;
and their mind never treats unlearned bodhisattvas with contempt.

Regarding the faults of others, whether real or unreal, one does not speak of them nor act with malice, nor seeks out their vulnerabilities; rather, one constantly and diligently cultivates loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Mañjuśrī!
"This is the practice of the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the śrāvakas,
which bodhisattvas should know. Mañjuśrī,
how should one know the practice of the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata for a bodhisattva?"

Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a person who, for some reason—whether a minor cause or a great cause, a minor undertaking or a great undertaking, a minor matter of importance or a great matter of importance—desired to pass beyond such worlds of atoms to reach that place.
He reflects thus:
"By means of which supernormal power can I pass beyond such worlds and reach that place?
Thereupon, that person reflects as follows:
"If I were now to rely upon the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata, I would be able to pass through such worlds and reach that place.
Mañjuśrī! Once that person has reflected thus, they immediately rely upon the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata and set out upon that path.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers swiftly traverse such worlds as these?
Mañjuśrī replied, “He can transcend it.
The Buddha said:
“In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not dwell in association with any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not draw near to any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not practice with any followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle; does not act as their kinsman; does not exchange wealth or goods with them; does not engage in the same spiritual practices; does not converse with them; and does not cohabit with them;”
Whether in a forest, in a monastery, or on a walking path, one does not practice in the same place [as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle];

one does not read or recite the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor contemplate or believe in the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle; and one does not instruct others to read or recite even a single verse thereof.
They do not read or recite that which is inconsistent with the Śrāvaka-yāna, nor do they teach it to others.
If such a person reads, they read the Mahāyāna; if they recite, they recite the Mahāyāna; they also teach others to read and recite the Mahāyāna, and whatever they speak, they speak of the Mahāyāna.
Such a person purifies their body, speech, and mind, and skillfully upholds the precepts; they also cause others to purify their body, speech, and mind and establish them in wholesome dharmas.

Toward those who practice the Mahāyāna—bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others who read, recite, and embrace the Mahāyāna—they honor them with right intention, following and training accordingly. They associate with them without abandoning them, relying upon and drawing near to them, making offerings according to the Dharma, regarding them as spiritual friends, and dwelling together with them.
Whether in the forest, in a monastery, or on a walking path, they practice together with them.

Toward those who belong to the Mahāyāna, who embrace the Mahāyāna, who have received the Mahāyāna, and who uphold the Mahāyāna, one should offer the highest respect and the most excellent worship—namely, lamps, various flowers, incense, powdered incense, ointments, and exquisite garlands for anointing the body—and thus make such offerings.
Such a person, having read and recited the Mahāyāna, with a mind of supreme joy teaches others to read and teaches others to recite it, never disparaging bodhisattvas who have not yet studied.
He establishes other bodhisattvas in their training, constantly speaking words of affection and words that are beautiful and sublime.

Such a person does not abandon the Mahāyāna even for the sake of losing their life or facing death; they always gather in all those who practice the Mahāyāna, study the Mahāyāna, read the Mahāyāna, recite the Mahāyāna, and uphold the Mahāyāna. Regarding them with the highest respect, they give rise to great joy and provide extensive offerings, and they also cause others to train in this way, possessing a profound and deep resolve.

Such a person is not hated by anyone and does not engage in contention with others; they constantly seek all sūtras never heard before, seeking them with a foremost, profound, and earnest mind, and always respecting with reverence those from whom they hear them.
One should conceive of such a person as a teacher and cause others to train in the same way; one should not disparage bodhisattvas who have not yet trained.

Whether the faults of others are real or unreal, one should neither speak of them nor misrepresent them, nor seek out their vulnerabilities; furthermore, one should teach others to train in this same manner.

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, a bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost the bodhicitta, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost the bodhicitta;

likewise, a bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva practices, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva practices.”

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the karma for awakening, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the karma for awakening;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the path of the bodhisattva, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the path of the bodhisattva;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost all the dignified conduct of a bodhisattva, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost all the dignified conduct of a bodhisattva.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s grasp, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s grasp;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost all the skillful means of a bodhisattva, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way those realms of sentient beings who have lost all the skillful means of a bodhisattva;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s intention, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s intention.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the power of the bodhisattva’s conditioned practices, and he also constantly teaches others to observe in this same way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the power of the bodhisattva’s conditioned practices;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s practice of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, and he also constantly teaches others to observe in this same way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s practice of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and he also constantly teaches others to observe in this same way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
In this way, the bodhisattva constantly practices giving themselves and also teaches others to give;
likewise, the bodhisattva does not wrong others themselves and also teaches others not to wrong others;

likewise, the bodhisattva constantly observes for themselves those realms of sentient beings who have lost the Buddha-dharma, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this same way those realms of sentient beings who have lost the Buddha-dharma.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who are devoid of the desire for wholesome dharmas, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who are devoid of the desire for wholesome dharmas;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings bound [by afflictions], and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings bound [by afflictions];

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings afflicted by illnesses that have persisted for a very long time, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings afflicted by illnesses that have persisted for a very long time.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the practice of the true Dharma, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the practice of the true Dharma;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the perfection of merit, wisdom, and so forth, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the perfection of merit, wisdom, and so forth;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the seeds of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the seeds of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of all sentient beings who are solitary, and also constantly teaches others to observe the realm of all such solitary sentient beings;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of all sentient beings who have long been asleep, and also constantly teaches others to observe the realm of all such sentient beings who have long been asleep;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of all sentient beings of inferior lineage, and also constantly teaches others to observe the realm of all such sentient beings of inferior lineage.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost faith in the Mahāyāna, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost faith in the Mahāyāna;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost their ethical discipline, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost their ethical discipline;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost the factors conducive to entry [into the path], and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost the factors conducive to entry.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost the practice of joy in patience, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost the practice of joy in patience;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realm of sentient beings who have lost the practice of joy in giving, self-control, and upholding the precepts, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realm of sentient beings who have lost the practice of joy in giving, self-control, and upholding the precepts.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost mindfulness in their mental conduct, yet possess contentment, shame, and remorse; he also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost mindfulness in their mental conduct, yet possess contentment, shame, and remorse.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the sequential entry into the path of the pāramitās; he also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the sequential entry into the path of the pāramitās.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the roots of goodness of the Buddha; he also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the roots of goodness of the Buddha.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost their spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and also constantly teaches others to observe in this same manner those realms of sentient beings who have lost their spiritual friends;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost the opportunity to benefit all sentient beings, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this same manner those realms of sentient beings who have lost the opportunity to benefit all sentient beings;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself those realms of sentient beings who have lost conformity with the Dharma (*dharmānulomika*), and also constantly teaches others to observe in this same manner those realms of sentient beings who have lost conformity with the Dharma.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who follow after the loss of wisdom, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who follow after the loss of wisdom;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who follow after the loss of meaning, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who follow after the loss of meaning;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the meaning of the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the meaning of the sūtras of definitive meaning.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the four right efforts, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the four right efforts;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of sentient beings who have lost the true Dharma and Vinaya, speech, and good conduct, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of sentient beings who have lost the true Dharma and Vinaya, speech, and good conduct;

in this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself the realms of impoverished sentient beings, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this way the realms of impoverished sentient beings.

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly observes for himself that universal loving-kindness pervades all worlds, and also constantly teaches others to observe in this same way that universal loving-kindness pervades all worlds.
They have such a thought:
"Those sentient beings are without a protector and without a refuge;
those sentient beings are all ablaze with flames."
All those sentient beings have no refuge;
all those sentient beings have no protector;
all those sentient beings are in total ignorance.
"At what time shall I be able to act as their master, to provide them with refuge, to provide them with a dwelling, to provide them with protection, and to provide them with the light of a lamp?
"Mañjuśrī! [the Buddha said.]

It is like a great king of the garuḍas who is youthful, vigorous, and possesses great strength; whatever he desires in his mind, he can fly up to the summit of Mount Sumeru, then descend into the great ocean, seize the female nāgas, and lift them up into the air.
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva who practices the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers possesses the power of great merit and roots of goodness; with swift and vigorous momentum, wherever there is an assembly of the Tathāgatas, he can reach it instantly according to his heart's desire."

They are able to reach all places of birth for sentient beings who have committed evil deeds in the various evil realms; they can act as their masters and provide them with a place of refuge, causing them to leave behind all evils, serving as their dwelling, their protection, and their lamp.
Mañjuśrī! This is the practice of the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers that bodhisattvas should know. Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many Tathāgatas in all the worlds of the ten directions as there are atoms of dust, doing so every single day for each and every Tathāgata;
Furthermore, suppose one were to take jewels filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in alms;
and if one were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, whatever merit might be gained therein— Mañjuśrī!

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings—equal in number to the atoms within all worlds of the ten directions—and cause them all to dwell in the fruit of a srotāpanna, Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to abide in the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds of the ten directions, such that they all attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin;
Mañjuśrī! whatever merit there might be in that—”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to dwell in the fruit of an Anāgāmin, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds of the ten directions, and cause them all to dwell in the fruit of an Anāgāmin—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to abide in the fruit of arhatship, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, and cause them all to dwell in the fruit of arhatship; Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to abide in the path of a pratyekabuddha, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, and cause them all to dwell in the path of a pratyekabuddha—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

If, moreover, there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes a single sentient being to abide in the bodhicitta of the sheep-vehicle practice, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, in the bodhicitta of the practice of the sheep-vehicle;
Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes a single sentient being to abide in the bodhicitta of the elephant-vehicle practice, this merit surpasses the former by more than incalculable times (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, in the bodhicitta that practices the elephant vehicle;
Mañjuśrī! [Whatever merit they might have]...”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes even a single sentient being to abide in the bodhicitta of the practice of the vehicle of the supernatural powers of the moon and sun, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cause all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, to abide in the bodhicitta of the practice of the vehicle of lunar and solar supernormal powers;
Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes a single sentient being to abide in the bodhicitta of the vehicle of the śrāvaka’s supernormal powers, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, so that they all dwelt in the bodhicitta of the practice of the vehicle of the śrāvaka’s supernormal powers;
Mañjuśrī! As for the merit they would possess—”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes even a single sentient being to abide in the bodhicitta of the practice of the Tathāgata’s vehicle of supernormal powers, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial robes and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with a single meal on a single day, gives it at one time to a single upāsaka—one who has entered the Three Refuges with faith, upholds the five precepts, and possesses a pure mind within the Buddha-dharma—this merit surpasses the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow divine garments and divine food of a hundred flavors upon as many upāsakas in all worlds of the ten directions as there are atoms of dust, who have entered the three refuges with faith, uphold the five precepts, and possess pure faith in the Buddha-dharma— if they were to constantly give in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
Mañjuśrī, whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, gives it as an offering at one time to the very first person among the eightfold assembly of monks, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon the very first person among the eightfold assembly in as many worlds in the ten directions as there are atoms of dust, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, at a single time, gives it as a gift to one *srotāpanna*, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many srotāpannas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, gives it as a gift once to a single Sakṛdāgāmin, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many Srotāpannas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day at a single time, gives it to a single Anāgāmin, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many non-returners (anāgāmin) as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

If, moreover, there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, at a single time, gives it as a gift to a single Arhat, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many Arhats as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—
Mañjuśrī, whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, gives it as an offering once to a single pratyekabuddha, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (asaṃkhyeya).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors, and every day bestow them upon as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, on a single day, offers a single meal at one time to a single sentient being—a Bodhisattva practicing the vehicle of sheep—this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

Whenever and with whatever object a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), at the very moment that mind arises, there is not a single unwholesome karma that is not abandoned, nor is there a single Buddha-dharma that does not arise.
Mañjuśrī! Thus does a bodhisattva achieve inconceivable merit. Mañjuśrī!

For example, just as the world-renowned king of birds, the kalaviṅka, while still within the shell of its egg before it has hatched, already surpasses all other flocks of birds with its deep resonance and beautiful song.
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening, though within the shell of ignorance and with eyes obscured, clouded, obstructed, and covered by the darkness of karma and afflictions, surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, for they are already able to grasp the roots of goodness and proclaim them through the wondrous sounds of vows and practices."

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many beings practicing the sheep-vehicle (*aurabhrika-yāna*) as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

If, moreover, there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with only a single meal on a single day, at a single time, bestows it upon a single sentient being who is a bodhisattva traveling by elephant-vehicle, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many beings practicing the elephant vehicle as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such giving for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges; Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess from this—”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, for the space of one month, offers a single meal once a day to a bodhisattva practicing the vehicle of supernatural powers, this merit would surpass the former by more than incalculable times (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many bodhisattvas practicing the vehicle of the moon-day supernatural powers as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions— and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges—
Mañjuśrī, whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, for a single day, offers a single meal at one time to a bodhisattva practicing the vehicle of the śrāvaka with supernormal powers, this merit would surpass the former by an incalculable amount (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow divine garments and divine food of a hundred flavors upon as many śrāvakas practicing the vehicle of supernatural powers as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions—and were to continue such giving constantly for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might thereby acquire;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with but a single meal on a single day, at a single time, gives alms to a single Bodhisattva practicing the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, this merit would surpass the former by more than incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) times.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon as many bodhisattvas practicing the vehicle of supernatural powers throughout all worlds in the ten directions as there are atoms in those worlds—and were to continue giving in this manner for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—whatever merit they might thereby acquire; Mañjuśrī!”

If, moreover, there should be any son of good family or daughter of good family who hears this Dharma-gate and, having heard it, gives rise to faith, their merit will surpass that of the former by more than incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) degrees.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to construct monasteries equal in number to the atoms of all worlds in the ten directions, and within each monastery were to establish and cause to dwell as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in a million trichiliocosms; and were to adorn the dwellings with necklaces fashioned from celestial Jambūnada gold, lightning-mani jewels, and genuine precious gems, and erect jeweled banners, hanging silk streamers and canopies—”
It was draped all around with curtains made of nets of *vaiḍūrya* jewel-kings and hung with tinkling bells;

it was everywhere anointed with *nāgakesara* sandalwood. Various kinds of exquisite flowers were scattered about, such as *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, *mahāmañjūṣaka*, *pāriyātraka*, *tāraṇī*, *vitāraṇī*, *bala*, *sugandha*, *dhanuṣkārika*, celestial *sumana*, *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*.

If one were to offer divine, exquisite garments and divine food of a hundred flavors to pratyekabuddhas every day, continuing in this manner for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, making such offerings at all times—whatever merit would result from that; [it would not equal the merit of one who hears this Dharma].

Mañjuśrī! If there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who hears the name of the Buddha, the name of the Omniscient One, or the name of the Tathāgata, the name of the Lord of the World, and either recites it themselves or sees a painted image, or even an image made of clay, wood, or other materials—the merit of this would surpass that of the former by more than incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) times; how much more so if they join their palms in reverence?

This merit is already more than incalculable (asaṃkhyeya); how much more so for one who further offers lamps, flowers, incense, and unguents, or even speaks of all virtues with their mouth—the resulting merit becomes increasingly superior and increasingly vast.
Thereupon, they will successively receive great wealth and happiness, until finally they attain all-knowledge. "Mañjuśrī!

It is like a single drop of extremely minute water falling into the great ocean; it is neither exhausted nor diminished, even until the time when the great fire at the end of the kalpa burns everything away."

"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī! If one plants even the most minimal roots of goodness toward the Tathāgata, they will not be exhausted nor diminished, until the fire of the knowledge of all-knowledge arises."

Mañjuśrī! For example, the lunar disc surpasses all the stars; it is foremost in its majesty and possesses abundant radiance, for its substance is perfectly full—namely, lofty, vast, preeminent, and expansive.
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!

Even the most subtle and minute roots of goodness of a Tathāgata surpass all other roots of goodness; they possess abundant radiance and a perfected essence, being what is called lofty, vast, supreme, and expansive."
Mañjuśrī! In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished inconceivable merit. Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to daily bestow celestial robes and celestial food of a hundred flavors upon all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, and all Śrāvakas in all worlds throughout the ten directions—numbering as many as the atoms of dust in those worlds—and were to continue such giving for as long as the kalpas of the Ganges River;
Mañjuśrī, as for the merit of all such giving:

Furthermore, if there should be any son of good family or daughter of good family who hears this Dharma-gate and, having heard it, gives rise to faith, their merit shall surpass that of the former by more than incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) degrees.
How much more so for one who personally transcribes it or causes others to transcribe it; this merit is even more superior, surpassing incalculable numbers (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Because this merit serves as the cause for realizing the wisdom of a Buddha, it is therefore supreme.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who were to seize or steal the robes or food belonging to immeasurable and innumerable śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, Mañjuśrī! [what would be the mass of their transgressions?]”

Furthermore, if there should be another man or woman who, with a mind of hatred and malice, seizes or steals from a person who has faith in the Mahāyāna even as much as a single morning meal or a single midday meal, this sin exceeds the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

All the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present, throughout immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, have practiced giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom solely for the purpose of severing the afflictions within their own bodies.
The Bodhisattva is not like that!
Even if they give away as little as a single morsel of food to an animal, it is all for the purpose of ensuring that the seeds of the Triple Gem are never severed.
"Mañjuśrī! [he said].

If there is a man or a woman who, with a mind of hatred, destroys the immeasurable and innumerable aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation belonging to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and destroys their aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—if they continue to destroy in this manner for the duration of kalpas, such is the mass of their transgressions.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be any man or woman who, with a mind of hatred and malice, destroys the single precept of Mahāyāna faith belonging to even one bodhisattva, or causes another to destroy it—even down to a single precept—this transgression is more numerous than that by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

All the accumulations of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are solely for the purpose of severing the afflictions within their own bodies.
The Bodhisattva is not like that!

Even the mass of merit from a single day or a single precept is dedicated entirely to severing all evil karma—the causes for sentient beings to fall into the miserable realms—and even to realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who bound all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions within prisons, such that they accumulated a mass of all possible offenses; Mañjuśrī!”

Furthermore, if there should be another man or woman who conceives a mind of malice toward a bodhisattva, not even looking at them but instead twisting their body and turning their face away, this transgression exceeds the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.
“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who plucked out all the eyes of all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, Mañjuśrī! [the accumulation of their sin would be great].”

Furthermore, if there should be any man or woman who, with a mind of hatred and malice, does not look upon a Bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna, this transgression would exceed that former one by an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions were to lose their sight for as many eons as there are. Mañjuśrī!”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a heart of loving-kindness, compassionately desires that all sentient beings obtain eyes, and continues this for the duration of kalpas; Mañjuśrī! As for the merit they would thereby possess; [it would be immeasurable].

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with a pure mind, gazes upon a bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to cause all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions to open their prisons and release them from their bonds, and furthermore cause them to become wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*) and enjoy the peace and happiness of their kingdoms, and furthermore cause them to abide in the bliss of Śakra, King of Devas—whatever merit this may bring, [it does not equal the merit of one who upholds the name of the Buddha].”

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who, with a pure mind, desires to see a bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna, and with a pure mind praises that bodhisattva, this merit surpasses the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions in the path of the pratyekabuddhas, Mañjuśrī, whatever merit they might possess;”

Furthermore, if there should be another son of good family or daughter of good family who causes a single bodhisattva who believes in the Mahāyāna to increase their Buddha-seed even to the extent of a single root of goodness, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna and is able to establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions in the bodhicitta, whatever merit they may possess; Mañjuśrī!...”

If there should be yet other bodhisattvas who have faith in the Mahāyāna and do not seek material sustenance, even if they recite but a single verse in its entirety, this merit would surpass that of the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who caused as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions to fall into the hells or the animal realm for the duration of an eon; Mañjuśrī! [the merit of one who hears this Dharma would surpass that of the former.]”

Furthermore, if there should be another man or woman who cuts off the bodhicitta of a single bodhisattva, and that bodhicitta is thus severed, this transgression is more numerous than the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who were to sever the bodhicitta of all sentient beings—equal in number to the atoms of all worlds in the ten directions—and thereby cause that bodhicitta to be destroyed, Mañjuśrī! [the mass of their sin would be as follows:]”

Furthermore, if there should be another man or woman who severs the faith in the Mahāyāna of even a single sentient being, thereby severing their practice of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, this transgression is greater than the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions were born in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and Yama’s abode.

Mañjuśrī! If there were a bodhisattva who could cause all such sentient beings to emerge from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and Yama, and establish them in the bodhicitta—Mañjuśrī! whatever merit they might possess; Mañjuśrī!

If there should be another bodhisattva who causes even a single sentient being to have faith in the Mahāyāna and enter the Mahāyāna, this merit would surpass the former by more than an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who could cause as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions to turn back from their path, Mañjuśrī, such would be the mass of their accumulated sin;”

Furthermore, if there should be any man or woman who causes even a single bodhisattva who has faith in the Mahāyāna to regress, this transgression is greater than that by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a man or a woman who, regarding as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, gave rise to a mind of jealousy toward their offerings and material gains, and by cutting off the causes and conditions for those offerings and gains, spoke evil words and slandered them in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, failing to praise those Pratyekabuddhas—Mañjuśrī! whatever mass of sin that person has accumulated;”

Furthermore, if there should be another man or woman who, out of a mind of jealousy toward a bodhisattva who believes in the Mahāyāna, cuts off the causes and conditions for that person’s offerings and material gains by failing to praise them, this transgression exceeds the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amount.

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, were to give even a small amount of water—so little as a single small jar—with a pure mind to one who has faith in the Mahāyāna, they would obtain the karmic fruit and retribution of the roots of goodness and merit acquired by a single Bodhisattva, namely, the wealth and happiness of an asaṃkhyeya realm of a universal wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin). How much more so for giving to a Bodhisattva who diligently reads and recites the Mahāyāna sūtras; this merit surpasses the former by an asaṃkhyeya.”

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, those bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the World-Honored One taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Entering the Seal of Non-Entrance into Samādhi.
